source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
finding: Two necessary conditions for skilled intuition: an environment with sufficiently valid cues (stable, in principle specifiable cue-outcome links) and an adequate chance to learn those cues. Intuition is defined as recognition (Simon 1992).
numbers: Two conditions. Chess mastery cited at about 10,000 hours (Chase & Simon 1973); masters hold 50,000-100,000 patterns.
quote: Skilled intuitions will only develop in an environment of sufficient regularity, which provides valid cues to the situation.
limits: Conceptual synthesis by two authors, not a new experiment. 'Adequate' practice is not quantified. The authors disagree on how often the conditions fail.
agent_relevance: Trust in a fast first answer should be a function of two checkable facts about the task class: is it regular, and has the agent had feedback on it. Not a function of how confident the answer feels.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
finding: Validity is a property of the environment (its causal and statistical structure), not of the person. High validity does not mean no uncertainty: poker, bridge and warfare are high-validity but uncertain, because skill still raises the odds.
numbers: Examples: fireground collapse cues and neonatal sepsis cues = fairly high validity; individual stock prices and long-term political forecasts = effectively zero validity.
limits: Validity classes are asserted by argument. The authors admit that judging validity is not always easy (Tetlock needed 15 years to show forecasting was near zero).
agent_relevance: Define task-class validity as 'does a better answer reliably raise the success rate', not 'is the task deterministic'. Probabilistic tasks (games, noisy puzzles) can still be trustable.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
finding: Subjective confidence is not a usable marker. No feeling separates a skilled intuition from a heuristic one; a single answer comes to mind in both cases. Confidence tracks the internal consistency of the evidence, not its quality.
numbers: Cites Einhorn & Hogarth 1978, Griffin & Tversky 1992, Arkes 2001 for the weak confidence-accuracy link.
quote: There is no subjective marker that distinguishes correct intuitions from intuitions that are produced by highly imperfect heuristics.
limits: Claim rests on cited work, not a new test. Klein adds that experts who face direct consequences may be better calibrated.
agent_relevance: Do not gate on the model's stated or felt confidence alone. Gate on external track record by task class plus code-checkable signals. Agrees with guardrail G1 but says the signal must not be self-reported confidence.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
finding: The safe test of any judgment, one's own or another's, is the validity of the environment plus the judge's history of learning that environment.
numbers: Procedure has two inputs: environment validity and learning history.
limits: Both inputs are hard to measure in people. In an agent both can be logged.
agent_relevance: Nearly an operational rule: keep a per-task-class record (regularity estimate, number of graded past cases, hit rate of first answers) and use it to choose fast answer versus deliberate.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
finding: Learning conditions spelled out: prolonged practice and feedback that is rapid and unequivocal. Feedback that is delayed, sparse or ambiguous breeds overconfidence even when short-term feedback is good.
numbers: Finance, psychotherapy, intelligence analysis: short-term feedback ample, long-term feedback delayed, sparse, ambiguous.
limits: Delay and ambiguity have no numeric thresholds.
agent_relevance: Track feedback quality per task class: latency and unambiguity of grading. A class with delayed or fuzzy grading should not earn 'trusted fast answer' status even after many cases.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
finding: Fractionated expertise: the same professional is expert at some tasks and not others. Nurses, physicians and auditors appear on both Shanteau's good-performance and poor-performance lists. Auditors do well on hard data, worse on fraud cues. Forecasters do better on temperature and precipitation than on hail.
numbers: Three professions on both lists (Shanteau 1992). Hail versus routine weather (Stewart, Roebber & Bosart 1997).
limits: Examples are anecdotal or from cited work. The authors call fractionation 'the rule, not an exception'.
agent_relevance: Track record must be at the level of task class, not 'the agent is good at math'. A trusted class can sit next to an untrusted one in the same domain.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
finding: Experts' defence against overreach is recognising anomalies and novelty: true expertise includes noticing that a case fits no familiar category and switching to deliberate search. Klein's experts (weather, engineering, logistics) refuse questions outside their competence.
numbers: Contrast: Klein sees experts as less prone to overconfidence; Kahneman sees fractionation producing the illusion of validity.
quote: The ability to recognize that a situation is anomalous and poses a novel challenge is one of the manifestations of authentic expertise.
limits: The main place the two authors differ in emphasis; the paper does not settle it with data.
agent_relevance: A familiarity/typicality check on the input (is this case like the graded past cases?) is the agent version of anomaly detection. Out-of-class inputs should lose fast-answer rights.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
finding: Where intuitions come from when skill is absent: heuristics. Three illustrations: the bat-and-ball item, anchoring, and attribute substitution (reading age to GPA).
numbers: Bat-and-ball: about 50% intuitive errors at MIT, Princeton, Harvard; about 90% at less selective schools (Frederick 2005). Anchoring: expected gap of $35,000 between $100,000 and $30,000 anchors, half the anchor gap (Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995).
limits: Lab puzzles; the authors argue anchoring also appears in courtrooms and real estate.
agent_relevance: For a language model, a fluent first answer on a trap problem is the analogue of the 10-cent answer. A cheap check (substitute back) beats trusting it. Class-level hit rates on trap-style items would flag these.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
finding: Meehl paradigm as summarised: Meehl (1954) reviewed about 20 studies and simple statistical models beat clinicians in almost every case even with less information. Goldberg (1970) bootstrapping: models of 29 clinicians beat the clinicians. Karelaia & Hogarth (2008) tie the effect mainly to inconsistency.
numbers: Meehl: about 20 studies. Goldberg: 29 clinicians, 861 patients, 11 MMPI scales, psychotic versus neurotic.
limits: Second-hand summary; Meehl, Goldberg and Karelaia & Hogarth were not opened here.
agent_relevance: Noise (inconsistency) is a separate failure from bias. Sampling the same model several times and averaging by code is the agent's analogue of the bootstrap model.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
finding: Their reading of the Grove et al. 2000 meta-analysis: algorithms do not win because people are inept. They win in low-validity settings where weak cues must be found and used consistently, and also in very high validity settings where lapses matter.
numbers: Grove et al. as cited: 136 studies; mechanical better in 63, tie in 65, clinical better in 8. Gaps of 17+ effect-size points for college grades, throat infection, GI diagnosis, hospital stay, job turnover, suicide attempts, delinquency, malingering, occupational choice.
quote: people perform significantly more poorly than algorithms in low-validity environments.
limits: Counts are as reported by K&K; the primary Grove paper could not be opened in this session.
agent_relevance: Two regimes where a rule or code should replace the model's own judgment: very noisy tasks and very regular tasks. Only the middle band (regular but too complex to hand-code, with feedback) favours trusting skilled intuition.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
finding: Algorithms need stringent conditions: adequate variable list, reliable measurable criterion, a body of similar cases, cost-benefit that justifies building it, and low chance of changed conditions. Humans must supervise because of automation bias.
numbers: Five conditions (a to e). Automation bias from Skitka, Mosier & Burdick 1999, 2000.
limits: The authors split on how often these hold.
agent_relevance: The same five conditions say when a task class has enough graded cases for a track record to mean something. A class with few cases or shifting rules cannot earn trust.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: A failure to disagree
finding: Semi-formal middle path both agree on: the premortem (Klein 2007). The team imagines the plan failed and writes reasons for two minutes, using prospective hindsight to unlock dissent.
numbers: Two minutes; reasons collected round the table starting with the leader.
limits: The paper gives no outcome data for the premortem.
agent_relevance: A cheap one-shot doubt move; compare with G1, which forbids scheduled doubt. Use only on classes with an untrusted track record.

source: Kuncel, Klieger, Connelly & Ones (2013) Mechanical versus clinical data combination in selection and admissions decisions: a meta-analysis
finding: Across work and academic prediction, mechanically combining the same predictors beat expert holistic combination, even when experts knew the job and had extra information.
numbers: 25 samples in 17 studies. Job performance r=.44 mechanical vs .28 clinical (more than 50% improvement). Advancement .42 vs .36. Training .31 vs .16. GPA .58 vs .48. Other academic outcomes .47 vs .46 (clinical n=161). About 2,263 mechanical and 2,027 clinical worker predictions; 889 and 632 student predictions.
quote: people are effective at collecting information but appear to be less effective at combining multiple sources of information into a final decision.
limits: Few studies. Some multiple-R values are inflated by shrinkage; with the strictest shrinkage the advantage vanished but did not reverse for two criteria. No range-restriction correction. File-drawer risk acknowledged.
agent_relevance: Experts are fine at collecting information, weak at combining it. In the agent: let the model extract evidence, let code combine and decide.

source: Kuncel et al. (2013), lens model section
finding: Lens-model explanation of why holistic judgment loses: judges weight cues less than optimally and apply even their own weights unreliably; unique insight beyond the linear model (C) is typically near zero.
numbers: Parameters: Rs (consistency of the judge's strategy), G (match to the optimal linear model), C (unmodelled knowledge, usually about 0). Cites Karelaia & Hogarth 2008 for C near 0.
limits: Lens model assumes linear cue use and a stable criterion; it may understate real nonlinear skill in kind domains such as chess.
agent_relevance: Formal model for the gating decision: if an answer is a noisy function of usable cues, averaging or rule-based combination beats a single draw. Where C is large (nonlinear pattern skill), the rule is wrong.

source: Aegisdottir et al. (2006) The meta-analysis of clinical judgment project: fifty-six years of accumulated research on clinical versus statistical prediction
finding: Statistical prediction was modestly better than clinical in mental health. An independent second large meta-analysis alongside Grove et al.
numbers: 67 studies, 92 effect sizes (173 with outliers). Most conservative set: 48 effects; 52% favoured statistical, 38% no difference, 10% favoured clinical. Cross-validated, outliers removed: d+ = -.12 (r+ = -.06), CI -.14 to -.09, stated as about 13% accuracy gain. Violence: r = -.09, about 90 more correct per 1,000.
limits: Effect is small. Heterogeneity Q significant except after removing outliers. Mental-health prediction only. Authors say the gain is 'not overwhelming'.
agent_relevance: Even in low-validity human-judgment domains the gap is small to moderate. Do not over-engineer replacement of the model; use rules where a graded track record shows a gain.

source: Aegisdottir et al. (2006), moderator results
finding: Moderators: familiarity with the prediction setting did not help clinicians (they did worse); giving clinicians the same or more information than the formula did not close the gap; experts did better than non-experts and matched formulas; supplying base rates moved clinicians close to formula accuracy.
numbers: Violence and academic performance clearly favoured formulas; treatment length predicted equally by both. All formula types except logically constructed rules beat clinicians; logic rules drew.
limits: Expert and base-rate results are trends flagged by the authors as needing replication; some cells are small.
agent_relevance: Base-rate injection is a cheap code-side move: give the model the prior hit rate of the task class before it answers. Graded expertise bridges to formula-level accuracy.

source: Gruning & Krueger (2021) The experience heuristic: review of Soyer & Hogarth, The Myth of Experience
finding: Restates Hogarth's kind versus wicked distinction: kind environments give swift, accurate, cheap feedback; wicked ones do not. People treat wicked environments as kind and overvalue experience. The reviewers cross confidence with validity into four cells, including the underconfident cell (valid experience, low confidence) that the book ignores.
numbers: Four cells: valid+confident, valid+unsure, invalid+confident (the dangerous one), invalid+unsure (fitting scepticism). Expertise is treated as two dimensions: performance and calibration.
limits: Book review, not data.
agent_relevance: The gate must be two-sided. Distrusting a first answer in a kind class wastes budget; trusting it in a wicked class loses accuracy.

source: Hogarth (2001) Educating Intuition, as reported by Kahneman & Klein 2009
finding: Origin of the 'wicked environment' idea: regularities that can be observed are misleading, so wrong intuitions develop. Example: a physician who palpated patients' tongues to confirm typhoid hunches without washing his hands, so his hunches came true by infecting them.
numbers: One example. Book not opened; known here only through K&K and the 2021 review.
limits: Hogarth, Lejarraga & Soyer (2015, Current Directions in Psychological Science 24:379) could not be fetched this session.
agent_relevance: Feedback can be contaminated by the agent's own actions or selection. A track record built from outcomes the agent influenced may be wicked. Log whether grading was independent of the agent's output.

source: Shanteau (1992) Competence in experts: the role of task characteristics, as reported by Kahneman & Klein 2009
finding: Experts do well in static, repeatable tasks with predictable outcomes and feedback (livestock judges, astronomers, test pilots, soil judges, chess masters, physicists, mathematicians, accountants, grain inspectors, photo interpreters, insurance analysts). They do poorly in dynamic, behavioural tasks (stockbrokers, clinical psychologists, psychiatrists, admissions officers, court judges, personnel selectors, intelligence analysts).
numbers: Eleven domains with expertise versus seven without, as listed by K&K.
limits: Not opened. Domain-level list ignores fractionation inside domains.
agent_relevance: Source for a feature checklist the agent could score per task class: static versus dynamic stimuli, repeatable, outcome predictable, feedback present.

source: Meehl (1954) Clinical versus statistical prediction, as reported by Kahneman & Klein 2009
finding: Founding source of the clinical versus actuarial contest. About 20 studies; statistical rules matched or beat clinicians in almost every case although the rules used a subset of the information. Meehl blamed partly base-rate neglect.
numbers: About 20 studies; outcomes from academic success to recidivism and violence.
limits: Not opened. Early studies were small.
agent_relevance: Earliest evidence that a rule using few cues can beat a holistic judge with more information.

source: Tetlock, Mellers, Rohrbaugh & Chen (2014) Forecasting tournaments: tools for increasing transparency and improving the quality of debate
finding: A low-validity domain (geopolitical forecasting; experts once shown no better than newspaper readers) where a tournament with scoring and feedback let selected and trained forecasters improve. Validity can be partly manufactured by scoring and fast feedback.
numbers: IARPA tournament, 200+ questions, Brier score. Best aggregation on the right side of 50/50 on 86.2% of daily forecasts; beat the control mean by 60% and other teams by 40%. Gains: selection about 10%, debiasing training about 10%, teams and markets about 10%, log-odds extremizing about 35% over the unweighted mean.
limits: Summary written by the project leaders. Extremizing gain is for aggregated human forecasts; our G4 forbids extremizing votes from one model because its samples are correlated.
agent_relevance: Task classes can be moved from wicked to kind by adding fast graded feedback. Before trusting a first answer, build graded history on the class; 'no feedback available' is itself a reason to deliberate or defer.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false when options are shown in lettered format; calibration improves with size and few-shot prompts. A model can score its own sample as P(True), better when shown several of its own samples. A trained P(IK) predicts whether the model can answer, but is poorly calibrated out of distribution.
numbers: Tasks: TriviaQA, Lambada, GSM8k, HumanEval, arithmetic, function synthesis. P(IK) trained on TriviaQA only: out-of-distribution AUROC rises with model size, OOD calibration is mostly underconfident. 'None of the above' replacement reduced accuracy and calibration. RLHF policies look miscalibrated until temperature is adjusted.
limits: Anthropic 2022 models; P(IK) needs a trained value head; transfer across task classes is only partial.
agent_relevance: The machine analogue of track-record trust. Self-knowledge works inside a trained task class and weakens on new classes, which matches K&K: trust is class-specific. Our scaffold has no training, so the record must come from graded counts, not a trained head.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration: strategies for eliciting calibrated confidence scores from language models fine-tuned with human feedback
finding: For RLHF models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude), verbalised confidence is often better calibrated than token probabilities. Asking for several candidate answers with probabilities improves it further.
numbers: Expected calibration error cut by a relative 50% on TriviaQA, SciQ and TruthfulQA. ChatGPT, TruthfulQA: label-probability ECE 0.451. On TruthfulQA the AUC of most confidence methods stays between about 0.2 and 0.55. n=10 samples used.
limits: Calibration (ECE) is not discrimination (AUC); the paper notes a 50% guesser can have perfect ECE. Table cells were read from extracted text and may be misaligned.
agent_relevance: Verbalised confidence can be calibrated on average yet unable to tell which answer is wrong, K&K's warning in numbers. Use as a weak input, below track record.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? An empirical evaluation of confidence elicitation in LLMs
finding: Verbalised LLM confidence is overconfident, clustering at 80-100% and in multiples of 5 like human talk. Sampling several answers and measuring agreement helps. Failure prediction stays weak on tasks needing professional knowledge.
numbers: Five dataset types, five LLMs including GPT-4 and LLaMA 2 Chat. GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. GPT-4 average AUROC only 62.7%. White-box versus black-box AUROC gap narrow: 0.522 to 0.605. Best methods reach ECE about 0.028.
limits: QA and reasoning benchmarks only; no method won on every task; gains shrink with model scale.
agent_relevance: Their practical recipe is Top-K prompt, self-random sampling, average confidence. Agreement across samples (G4: a hint, not proof) beats a stated number but still fails on specialist tasks, i.e. in classes with low validity for the model.

source: Kuhn, Gal & Farquhar (2023) Semantic uncertainty: linguistic invariances for uncertainty estimation in natural language generation
finding: Entropy over meaning-clusters of sampled answers (semantic entropy) predicts correctness of free-form answers better than token entropy, lexical similarity or P(True), because different wordings can mean the same thing.
numbers: Evaluated by AUROC on TriviaQA and CoQA with OPT models from 2.7B to 30B; semantic entropy was top in the figures (AUROC axis range about 0.72 to 0.82 for TriviaQA at 30B). Needs sampling and a paraphrase detector.
limits: Read from figures and text; exact table values not extracted. Only OPT models, QA tasks, 2023.
agent_relevance: A code-computable, training-free gate: sample N answers, cluster by meaning, high entropy means deliberate. It measures the model's uncertainty, not environment validity, so it still needs the track record.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking the most common answer boosts accuracy. The share of paths agreeing with the final answer is strongly correlated with accuracy on GSM8K, so low consistency can mark low confidence.
numbers: GSM8K +17.9%, SVAMP +11.0%, AQuA +12.2%, StrategyQA +6.4%, ARC-challenge +3.9%. PaLM-540B zero-shot CoT on GSM8K 43.0 to 69.2 with 40 paths. Gains largely saturate at 5-10 paths.
limits: Consistency-accuracy link shown in one figure on one task. Samples from one model share errors (our G4), so consistency can be high and wrong.
agent_relevance: Consistency across samples is a cheap, code-computed stand-in for how stable an intuition is. It is evidence about the model's fluency, not environment validity; pair it with graded history.

source: Synthesis from K&K 2009, Kadavath 2022, Kuhn 2023, Wang 2023 (our inference, not a source)
finding: Candidate gate for S0: answer fast and stop only if the task class has (1) a graded track record with enough cases, (2) feedback that was fast and independent of the agent, (3) a regular, non-zero-validity structure, and (4) the current input is typical of the class and samples agree. Otherwise deliberate or run a code check.
numbers: Four tests. No source gives thresholds (case count, hit-rate floor); set them from our own bench data.
limits: Our inference; no paper tested such a gate on LLM agents. Two-sided error: too much deliberation wastes budget, and our own data showed forced doubt hurt (92% vs 75%).
agent_relevance: This is the schema's S0 gate. The sources support its shape but not its numbers.
